gloss_terse: Tail — the hind extremity of an animal; figuratively the lowest, weakest, or most insignificant part
gloss_readable: The noun זָנָב (zanav) denotes the tail of an animal, both literally and as a vivid figure for social and political insignificance. When God commands Moses to seize the serpent 'by the tail' (Exod 4:4), the physical sense is primary. But Deuteronomy 28:13, 44 transforms the image into a proverb of covenant status: obedience makes Israel 'the head,' disobedience makes her 'the tail.' Isaiah 9:14 explicitly glosses the metaphor — 'the elder and honored man is the head; the prophet who teaches lies is the tail.' Samson's foxes, tied tail to tail with torches (Judg 15:4), remain one of Scripture's most unforgettable images. Spanish 'cola' and French 'queue' serve for both literal and figurative uses.

senses.1: The literal tail of an animal — the physical hind appendage. Moses grasps the serpent by the tail (Exod 4:4), Samson ties foxes tail-to-tail with firebrands (Judg 15:4), and Isaiah describes the smoldering 'tails' (stumps) of two firebrands representing weakened kings (Isa 7:4). Spanish 'cola,' French 'queue,' and German 'Schwanz' all map directly.
senses.2: Figuratively, the lowest or most subordinate position in a social or political hierarchy, contrasted with 'head' (רֹאשׁ). Deuteronomy 28:13, 44 pairs head and tail as emblems of covenant blessing versus curse. Isaiah 9:14 [Eng. 9:15] identifies the tail as the false prophet who leads the people astray. The metaphor emphasizes powerlessness, dependency, and disgrace.

gloss_terse: Heber/Cheber — personal name meaning 'associate, companion'; borne by several Israelite men
gloss_readable: The proper name חֶבֶר (Chever) derives from the root חבר ('to join, associate') and is borne by at least four distinct individuals in Scripture. The most prominent is Heber the Kenite, husband of Jael, who had separated from the other Kenites and pitched his tent near Kedesh (Judg 4:11, 17). It was into his tent that Sisera fled, only to be killed by Jael (Judg 4:21; 5:24). Other bearers include a grandson of Asher listed in Jacob's family (Gen 46:17; Num 26:45), a Judahite connected to Soco (1 Chr 4:18), and a Benjaminite in the genealogy of Elpaal (1 Chr 8:17). Spanish and English both transliterate as 'Heber.'

senses.1: Heber the Kenite, husband of Jael, a descendant of Moses' father-in-law Hobab. He had separated from the main Kenite group and camped near Kedesh-naphtali (Judg 4:11, 17). His political neutrality between Jabin of Hazor and Israel sets the dramatic stage for Jael's decisive act (Judg 4:21; 5:24). Spanish 'Heber,' French 'Héber.'
senses.2: A grandson of Asher through Beriah, listed among the seventy who went down to Egypt (Gen 46:17). He is the eponymous ancestor of the Heberite clan (Num 26:45). Also the name of a man of Judah, father of Soco (1 Chr 4:18), and a Benjaminite descendant of Elpaal (1 Chr 8:17).

gloss_terse: Mother-in-law — a husband's mother or wife's mother, central to the Ruth narrative
gloss_readable: The noun חָמוֹת (chamot) specifically designates one's mother-in-law, and its occurrences cluster almost entirely in the book of Ruth, where the relationship between Naomi and Ruth is the emotional and theological heart of the story. Ruth's loyalty to her mother-in-law — 'your people shall be my people, your God my God' (Ruth 1:16) — redefines family beyond blood. The term appears at every turning point of the narrative: departure (Ruth 1:14), gleaning (2:11, 18-19, 23), and the threshing-floor plan (3:1, 6, 16-17). Micah 7:6 uses the same word in its portrait of social disintegration, where a daughter-in-law rises against her mother-in-law. Spanish 'suegra' and French 'belle-mère' both serve.

senses.1: A woman's mother-in-law, the mother of her husband. Dominates the book of Ruth, where Naomi is consistently called Ruth's chamot (Ruth 1:14; 2:11, 18-19, 23; 3:1, 6, 16-17), shaping the narrative's portrait of covenant loyalty across family lines. Micah 7:6 employs the same term in a prophecy of domestic betrayal where natural family bonds collapse. Spanish 'suegra,' German 'Schwiegermutter,' and French 'belle-mère' all correspond precisely.

gloss_terse: Leavened bread — bread or food made with leaven, prohibited during the Feast of Unleavened Bread
gloss_readable: The adjective-turned-noun חָמֵץ (chamets) denotes leavened bread or any food product containing leaven. Its significance is primarily ritual: during Passover and the seven-day Festival of Unleavened Bread, all chamets must be removed from Israelite households (Exod 12:15; 13:3, 7). The prohibition extends to offerings placed on the altar — no grain offering may be made with leaven (Lev 2:11), though leavened loaves accompany the thanksgiving peace offering (Lev 7:13). The sacrificial blood must not be offered 'with leavened bread' (Exod 23:18; 34:25). Spanish 'pan leudado/con levadura' and English 'leavened bread' convey the ritual distinction that gives this word its force.

senses.1: Bread or any food product prepared with leaven (שְׂאֹר), categorically forbidden during Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread. Exodus 12:15 and 13:3, 7 mandate its complete removal from every household for seven days. The prohibition also governs sacrifice: no grain offering may contain leaven (Lev 2:11), and Passover blood must not be presented alongside chamets (Exod 23:18; 34:25). An exception exists for the thanksgiving peace offering, where leavened loaves are included (Lev 7:13). Spanish 'pan leudado' and French 'pain levé' mark the distinction.

gloss_terse: Hanun — personal name meaning 'favored, gracious'; an Ammonite king and two post-exilic builders
gloss_readable: The name חָנוּן (Chanun) means 'favored' or 'gracious,' from the root חנן. The most prominent bearer is Hanun son of Nahash, king of Ammon, who humiliated David's ambassadors by shaving half their beards and cutting their garments, provoking a devastating war (2 Sam 10:1-4; 1 Chr 19:2-6). His misjudgment — acting on the suspicion of his advisors rather than accepting David's genuine condolence — stands as a cautionary tale about political mistrust. Two other men named Hanun appear among Nehemiah's wall-builders: one repaired the Valley Gate (Neh 3:13) and another (possibly the same person) repaired a section near the armory (Neh 3:30). Spanish 'Hanún' and English 'Hanun' transliterate directly.

senses.1: Hanun son of Nahash, king of Ammon, who succeeded his father and disgraced David's envoys sent with condolences (2 Sam 10:1-4; 1 Chr 19:2-6). His provocation triggered a major military campaign in which Ammon and their Aramean allies were decisively defeated. The narrative illustrates how diplomatic insult can escalate into full-scale war.
senses.2: One or two men named Hanun who participated in rebuilding Jerusalem's walls under Nehemiah. One repaired the Valley Gate and a thousand cubits of wall (Neh 3:13); another (possibly the same) repaired a section as the sixth son of Zalaph (Neh 3:30). Spanish 'Hanún,' French 'Hanun.'

gloss_terse: Hanani — personal name meaning 'gracious, my grace'; borne by several priests, prophets, and leaders
gloss_readable: The name חֲנָנִי (Chanani) is a shortened form of Hananiah, meaning 'the LORD is gracious.' It identifies at least five distinct individuals. The seer Hanani rebuked King Asa of Judah for relying on Aram rather than on the LORD (2 Chr 16:7) and was imprisoned for it — a powerful example of prophetic boldness meeting royal hostility. His son Jehu ben Hanani prophesied against Baasha of Israel (1 Kgs 16:1, 7) and later against Jehoshaphat (2 Chr 19:2; 20:34). A Levitical musician named Hanani served in David's temple choir (1 Chr 25:4, 25). Nehemiah's brother Hanani brought news of Jerusalem's ruined state (Neh 1:2) and was later appointed co-governor of the city (Neh 7:2). Spanish 'Hanani' preserves the transliteration.

senses.1: Hanani the seer, father of the prophet Jehu. He confronted King Asa of Judah for his alliance with Ben-hadad of Aram and was thrown into prison (2 Chr 16:7-10). His prophetic ministry emphasized trust in the LORD over political alliances.
senses.2: Other bearers of the name: a Levitical musician in David's temple service (1 Chr 25:4, 25); Nehemiah's brother who reported Jerusalem's distress and was later entrusted with the city's governance (Neh 1:2; 7:2); and a priest who played instruments at the wall dedication (Neh 12:36). The name's frequency in post-exilic texts reflects its popularity in the restoration community.

gloss_terse: Delighting in, willing, desiring — verbal adjective describing one who takes pleasure in or is inclined toward
gloss_readable: The adjective חָפֵץ (chaphets) describes someone who delights in, desires, or is willing — a person whose inner disposition inclines them toward something. It appears in both positive and negative frames. David tells Solomon that God seeks a heart that is 'willing' (חָפֵץ) to seek him (1 Chr 28:9). The psalmist asks, 'Who is the one delighting in life?' (Ps 34:13 [Eng. 34:12]) and declares that God takes no delight in wickedness (Ps 5:5 [Eng. 5:4]). Psalm 35:27 speaks of those who 'delight in' the vindication of the righteous. The word also covers simple willingness: Jeroboam consecrated 'whoever was willing' as priests (1 Kgs 13:33), and Naboth's vineyard is offered 'if you are willing' (1 Kgs 21:6). Spanish 'que se deleita/quiere' and English 'delighting/willing' both serve.

senses.1: Delighting in, taking pleasure in — describing a person whose heart is drawn toward something good or worthy. God is not one 'delighting in' wickedness (Ps 5:5), the godly person 'delights in life' (Ps 34:13), and the LORD's supporters 'delight in' his servant's righteousness (Ps 35:27). David charges Solomon to serve God with a 'willing' heart (1 Chr 28:9). Spanish 'que se deleita en,' French 'qui prend plaisir à.'
senses.2: Willing, inclined, consenting — expressing readiness or desire to act, without the stronger connotation of deep delight. Jeroboam ordained 'whoever was willing' as priest (1 Kgs 13:33), and Ahab offers Naboth an alternative vineyard 'if you are willing' (1 Kgs 21:6). This shade of meaning focuses on volitional consent rather than emotional pleasure.

gloss_terse: Magician, diviner-priest — a learned practitioner of ritual magic in Egyptian and Babylonian courts
gloss_readable: The noun חַרְטֹם (chartom) designates a class of learned magician-priests attached to the royal courts of Egypt and Babylon. In Egypt, Pharaoh summons his chartummim to interpret his dreams (Gen 41:8, 24) and to replicate Moses' signs (Exod 7:11, 22; 8:3 [Eng. 8:7]). They manage to match the first two plagues but fail at the gnats, conceding 'this is the finger of God' (Exod 8:14-15 [Eng. 8:18-19]), and are themselves afflicted with boils (Exod 9:11). In Daniel, the same term reappears for the Babylonian court magicians whom Daniel outperforms tenfold (Dan 1:20; 2:2). The word likely derives from Egyptian hry-tp ('chief lector-priest'). Spanish 'magos' and English 'magicians' are standard renderings.

senses.1: An Egyptian court magician or lector-priest skilled in sacred texts and ritual magic. Pharaoh's chartummim attempt to interpret dreams (Gen 41:8, 24) and duplicate the signs of Moses and Aaron through their secret arts (Exod 7:11, 22; 8:3, 14-15). Their progressive failure — replicating blood and frogs but not gnats — dramatizes the superiority of God's power. They are struck with boils along with all Egypt (Exod 9:11). Spanish 'magos,' French 'magiciens.'
senses.2: A Babylonian court diviner or ritual specialist, grouped with astrologers, sorcerers, and Chaldeans in the Babylonian wisdom establishment. Daniel and his companions are found ten times better than all such practitioners (Dan 1:20), and the chartummim cannot interpret Nebuchadnezzar's dream (Dan 2:2). The continuity of the term across Egyptian and Babylonian settings suggests a recognized ancient Near Eastern professional category.

gloss_terse: Harim — personal name meaning 'consecrated/devoted'; priestly and lay families in post-exilic Judah
gloss_readable: The name חָרִם (Charim) likely derives from a root meaning 'consecrated' or 'snub-nosed' (the latter a physical characteristic). It identifies both priestly and lay families prominent in the post-exilic community. A priestly house of Harim received the third lot in David's temple organization (1 Chr 24:8) and reappears in the return from exile (Ezra 2:39; Neh 7:42; 12:15). Members of this priestly family were among those who had married foreign wives (Ezra 10:21). A separate lay family of Harim also returned from Babylon (Ezra 2:32; Neh 7:35), with members likewise involved in the intermarriage crisis (Ezra 10:31). A Harim sealed the covenant under Nehemiah (Neh 10:5, 27). Spanish 'Harim' and English 'Harim' transliterate uniformly.

senses.1: The priestly family of Harim, assigned the third division in David's organization of temple service (1 Chr 24:8). Descendants returned from exile (Ezra 2:39; Neh 7:42) and appear in the priestly registry of Joiakim's generation (Neh 12:15). Some members were found guilty of intermarriage with foreign women (Ezra 10:21). A representative sealed the Nehemiah covenant (Neh 10:5).
senses.2: A lay family of Harim whose members also returned from Babylon (Ezra 2:32; Neh 7:35). Like the priestly family, some were implicated in the foreign-marriage reform (Ezra 10:31). A representative of this family signed the community covenant (Neh 10:27), and one member, Malchijah son of Harim, helped rebuild the wall and the Tower of the Ovens (Neh 3:11).

gloss_terse: To slaughter, butcher — killing an animal for food or sacrifice; extended to violent killing of people
gloss_readable: The verb טָבַח (tavach) means to slaughter or butcher, primarily describing the killing of animals for consumption. Joseph orders his steward to 'slaughter an animal and prepare' a feast (Gen 43:16), Lady Wisdom 'has slaughtered her meat' for the banquet of understanding (Prov 9:2), and the stolen ox is 'slaughtered' by the thief (Exod 22:1 [Eng. 21:37]). Deuteronomy 28:31 envisions the covenant curse of watching one's ox slaughtered before one's eyes. The verb extends to the violent slaughter of people in contexts of war and judgment: Lamentations 2:21 mourns the young and old 'slaughtered' in Jerusalem's streets, and Ezekiel 21:15 [Eng. 21:10] speaks of a sword polished 'for slaughter.' Spanish 'degollar/matar' and French 'égorger' capture the visceral force.

senses.1: To slaughter or butcher an animal for food, a feast, or sacrifice. Joseph commands that a beast be slaughtered for a banquet (Gen 43:16), Wisdom slaughters her meat (Prov 9:2), a thief slaughters a stolen ox (Exod 22:1), and the covenant curse threatens livestock slaughtered before the owner's helpless eyes (Deut 28:31). Also 1 Samuel 25:11, where Nabal's provisions include meat he has butchered. Spanish 'degollar/matar,' French 'égorger.'
senses.2: To slaughter people violently, as in warfare or divine judgment. Lamentations 2:21 mourns youths and elders slaughtered in the streets of fallen Jerusalem. Ezekiel 21:15 [Eng. 21:10] describes a sword sharpened and polished 'for the slaughter.' The same brutal imagery underlies Jeremiah 25:34 (shepherds led to slaughter) and Isaiah 34:2. The semantic range from kitchen to battlefield underscores the raw violence of the metaphor.
